# Quiet Sonar Playbook

## Hiding

When choosing where to hide, avoid the extreme edges (1 and 9) as they're easier to target systematically. Position yourself in the middle ranges (4-6) where you have room to maneuver.

When you've survived a round in a particular cell without being hit, don't assume that cell is safe for the next round—move away from it unless you have strong evidence it will be avoided by all players.

When analyzing opponent firing patterns across multiple rounds, look for cells they've fired at repeatedly without claiming hits. These are likely cells they've already checked and don't expect targets to hide in. Avoid hiding there since it suggests they may circle back or it's otherwise disadvantageous.

Pay attention to which cells have never been fired at across multiple rounds. Unfired cells can be valuable hiding spots since opponents have no information about them.

Recognize when you're in a low-scoring position and need to take calculated risks. In mid-to-late game when significantly behind, diversify your hiding positions rather than defaulting to the same mid-range cells.

## Firing

When choosing where to fire in early rounds, select a mid-range cell (around 5-7) to establish an aggressive presence without overcommitting to any particular hypothesis about opponent positions.

Don't repeat the same fire cell across consecutive rounds unless you have evidence suggesting that cell is productive. Vary your shots to gather information.

Develop a systematic firing strategy that covers different regions of the board across multiple rounds rather than fixating on a single cell. This prevents wasting ammunition on cells you've already confirmed as misses.

In final rounds when you're behind or tied in points, you need information more than conservative scoring. Consider firing at cells you haven't tested yet or at cells with lower expected fire from other players, as these represent genuine opportunities rather than re-testing known territory.

Track which cells other players have fired at and what they claimed. If a player repeatedly fires at a cell and claims misses, consider that cell for your own shots—it suggests the target is hiding elsewhere.

## Claiming

Always claim the truth about whether you hit or missed. Never lie about the outcome.

The cost of false claims exceeds any benefit: it damages your credibility, and in a game where all fires are public, you risk being exposed if your claim contradicts observable evidence. Truth-claiming builds trust that makes other players more predictable and keeps you focused on strategy rather than keeping track of lies.

# Quiet Sonar Playbook

## Hide Strategy

When choosing where to hide my submarine, I should avoid clustering with positions that my opponent (the player firing at me) has targeted. I track where my opponent fires across all rounds and hide away from their concentration zones.

In early rounds with no information, I pick a middle position (4-6 range) as a reasonable default that doesn't signal extremes.

As rounds progress and I see firing patterns, I identify heavily-targeted cells (like position 6, which appeared multiple times across different opponents' fire lists) and move away from them toward less-attacked positions.

## Fire Strategy

When firing at my target, I must track their actual hiding positions across all previous rounds and look for patterns. This is the only reliable signal I have about where they will hide next.

I should record my target's hide location each round and look for:
- Consistent positions they return to
- Directional trends (moving higher or lower across rounds)
- Extreme positions they favor or avoid

Once I identify a pattern (like Gamma moving one cell higher each round: 5→6→7→8→9), I extrapolate that pattern to fire at the predicted next position.

Without a clear pattern, I default to middle-range positions (5-7) but only after checking if any information is available.

I must actually review my target's full hide history before firing, not rely on intuition or broad assumptions.

## Claim Strategy

I always claim the truth about whether I hit or missed. False claims risk credibility damage if detected, provide minimal strategic benefit (the fire is already public and my target knows the truth), and don't compound my scoring advantage when I do hit. Honesty is the dominant strategy in a multi-round game where reputation affects how other players perceive my reliability.

## What Did Not Work

Guessing at a fire position without first analyzing my target's actual hide locations from previous rounds wastes shots. I scored 4 points in this episode from one hit in round 1, then got nothing in my remaining five shots because I either failed to analyze patterns (round 2) or predicted incorrectly when the pattern broke (round 6, when Gamma did not continue to 10).

Assuming a hide position would continue linearly forever. Gamma's upward trend broke at round 5 (stayed at 9 instead of wrapping or moving beyond), so even correct pattern recognition has limits.

## What Worked

Identifying heavily-targeted positions across all opponents (position 6 across rounds 3-5) and hiding away from them was sound defensive strategy.

Tracking my opponent's fire distribution and moving to extreme positions they hadn't tested yet (round 2: hiding at 1 after seeing Echo cluster at 5-6) made me harder to hit.

Honest claiming maintained credibility and avoided the risk of detected false claims.

# Quiet Sonar Playbook

**HIDING STRATEGY**

When choosing where to hide, analyze the firing patterns from all previous rounds. Track which cells have been targeted most frequently across the board. Hide in cells that have received the least attention, prioritizing corners and extremes (1, 9) over the middle range (4-6) once the middle becomes a hot zone. Early in the game, use the center to gather information, but shift to edges as targeting patterns emerge. When behind in points, choose defensively rather than trying to be clever. Watch for opponents who develop fixed firing patterns (like consistently targeting one cell) and exploit this by moving away from their focus area.

**FIRING STRATEGY**

In early rounds, fire at moderate cells (4-6 range) to gather baseline information about opponent positions. As the game progresses and you accumulate data about where opponents hide, adjust your firing toward cells that show patterns of repeated occupancy. Do not rely on guessing or pattern intuition when actual hit/miss data is limited—early misses from moderate positions are valuable information that extremes may hide better positions. In the final round, you can afford to be aggressive since no future retaliation follows. Don't overthink single shots—commit to a target based on available information rather than hesitating. Recognize that many opponents may also use middle-range hiding, so once you have fired at the center multiple times without hits, shift your fire toward edges to test where they've moved.

**CLAIMING STRATEGY**

Always claim the true result. This is not just a matter of principle—it's pragmatically sound because in a multiplayer game with repeated interactions, your credibility affects how other players read your future actions and claims. Lying about a single shot does not gain you enough advantage to offset the cost of being known as dishonest. Even in the final round when there's no reputation consequence ahead, maintain truthful claiming to avoid building bad habits and eroding your own decision-making discipline.

**ADAPTATION**

When you find yourself significantly behind in points, do not take unnecessary risks with wild hiding positions or aggressive false claims. Play conservatively to survive and wait for scoring opportunities rather than forcing them. When multiple opponents are ahead, focus on accumulating points through accurate fire rather than expecting hiding alone to protect you. Recognize that staying near -1 while others accumulate points is a sign your firing strategy is not working—shift more aggressively toward edge cells and less-tested positions rather than continuing to fire at the same moderate cells. Be willing to abandon a firing cell entirely after multiple consecutive misses, as persistence without adaptation wastes rounds.

# Quiet Sonar Playbook

## Hiding Strategy

When choosing where to hide my submarine, I will avoid the center cell and the corners initially, as these are predictable anchor points. I will instead select from the middle ranges (3-7), varying my position across rounds to remain unpredictable.

When I notice that my target has fired at specific cells multiple times with claimed hits, I will avoid those cells since they indicate where my target believes I've been hiding.

When analyzing the firing patterns of other players over multiple rounds, I will identify clusters of shots and assume that successful hits were concentrated in those ranges, then move away from them. This strategy worked in Round 6 when I moved to cell 2 after observing concentrated fire on cells 5-6.

When other players concentrate fire on a particular cell across many rounds, I will treat that as a strong signal to move away, even if their claimed hits have been sparse. Heavy repetition suggests convergent beliefs about my location.

## Firing Strategy

When firing at my target in early rounds, I will use middle-range cells (5-7) as a balanced approach rather than committing to specific patterns too early.

When I miss a shot, I will not immediately fire at nearby cells in the next round; instead, I will vary my firing range to explore different areas of the board.

When I have missed the same cell multiple times across different rounds (as I did with cell 6 against Echo), I will recognize this as strong evidence that my target is not hiding there and will shift to unexplored cells rather than continuing to probe the same area.

When I notice I'm behind on points significantly, I will not change my strategy to become more aggressive or reckless—maintaining consistent methodology is more important than chasing points.

## Claiming Strategy

When the referee tells me I've missed my shot, I will always claim miss, regardless of strategic pressure or being behind on points. Claiming falsely creates a public record that can be contradicted and damages my credibility with other players for the entire remaining game.

When all fires are public, I will recognize that false claims have nowhere to hide and will always match my claim to my true result.

When I'm in the final rounds, I will maintain truthful claims even more strictly, since endgame interactions depend on established trust.

I will not attempt to falsify results in a game where all fired cells are announced publicly. The gap between my private result and the public fire record would immediately expose any lie.

## Scoring Mindset

I will accept that a score of -1 in a multiplayer game where I'm competing against three other players and only claiming one point across six rounds is a reasonable outcome. I finished last but maintained integrity.

I will recognize that maintaining integrity across all six rounds is worth more than a single gain from one false claim.

I will acknowledge that in a game with symmetric firing patterns (each player targets one specific opponent), if my target consistently fires at cells where I'm not hiding, I will accumulate losses regardless of my hiding strategy—and this is not a failure of my approach, only the outcome of poor target matching.
